title: Hematocrit / PCV (Microhematocrit Method)

references.label: Standard clinical hematology laboratory textbooks/manuals (e.g. Henry's Clinical Diagnosis and Management)
CLSI Standards for Clinical Laboratory Practice

purpose: To determine the packed cell volume (PCV/hematocrit) — the proportion of whole blood occupied by red blood cells — as a rapid indicator of red cell mass, commonly used to screen for anemia or polycythemia and to cross-check an analyzer's hematocrit value.
principle: Anticoagulated whole blood is centrifuged in a narrow capillary tube at high speed; because red cells are denser than plasma, they pack at the bottom, leaving plasma above and a thin buffy coat (white cells/platelets) in between. The proportion of the tube occupied by packed red cells, read against a calibrated reading device or scale, is the hematocrit.
requiredMaterials: Heparinized (or EDTA, per local protocol) microhematocrit capillary tubes

procedure.instruction: Fill a capillary tube roughly two-thirds to three-quarters full with well-mixed anticoagulated whole blood.
Seal the dry end with sealing clay (or use a self-sealing tube per manufacturer instructions).

procedure.note: Balancing prevents tube breakage and uneven centrifugal force.
procedure.instruction: Load tubes into the microhematocrit centrifuge symmetrically (balanced), sealed end outward.
Centrifuge for the time/speed specified by the centrifuge manufacturer for complete red cell packing.

Read the packed red cell column against a hematocrit reading device immediately after centrifugation, measuring from the bottom of the red cell column to the top of the plasma meniscus (excluding the thin buffy coat).

observations: A distinct red cell column, thin buffy coat, and clear-to-straw-colored plasma column should be visible; grossly lipemic or hemolyzed plasma should be noted, as it can affect interpretation.
interpretation: Hematocrit is reported as a percentage (or fraction) of whole blood volume occupied by red cells; it correlates closely with hemoglobin (roughly 3× Hb in a normal, well-hydrated individual, though this ratio is a rule of thumb, not a fixed law) and is used alongside RBC count and indices, never interpreted alone.
precautions: Read immediately after centrifugation — plasma and cells can begin to remix or settle further over time.
Do not use expired or cracked capillary tubes.
limitations: Manual PCV can be affected by plasma trapping between packed cells, giving a slight overestimate; automated analyzer hematocrit (calculated from RBC count × MCV) is generally considered more precise for routine work, with manual PCV as a cross-check/backup method.
biosafetyNotes: Capillary tubes are a sharps/blood-exposure hazard — use puncture-resistant sealant handling technique and dispose of broken glass per sharps protocol.
